title: The k-th Group in the Dictionary

concept.title: Jump over whole blocks of groups by counting them
body: All groups of `k` numbers out of `1 .. n`, in increasing order inside a group, can be listed in dictionary order. We want the group at position `r` without listing the earlier ones. Decide the numbers from left to right. Suppose the next number can start from `x`. How many groups begin with `x` here? After taking `x`, we choose `k - 1` numbers from the `n - x` numbers larger than `x`: that is the binomial coefficient `C(n - x, k - 1)`.

If `r` is **larger** than this count, our group does not start with `x`: subtract the count from `r` and try `x + 1`. Otherwise `x` is the next number of our group, and we continue with `k - 1` numbers starting from `x + 1`.

The binomial table `c` comes from Pascal's triangle: `c[i][j] = c[i - 1][j - 1] + c[i - 1][j]`. `C(60, 30)` is about 1.2 * 10^17 and still fits in a 64-bit integer. Counting makes the search cost `O(n * k)` instead of `C(n, k)`.

statement: All groups of `k` different numbers chosen from `1, 2, ..., n` are written in dictionary order; inside a group the numbers are increasing. Given `n`, `k` and `r`, print the group at position `r` (the first group has position 1).
outputFormat: Print the `k` numbers of the group, separated by spaces.

examples.note: The order is 12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34, so the 5th group is 2 4.

hints: The groups that start with x are C(n - x, k - 1) in number.
If r is larger than that number, subtract it from r and try the next x.
Build a table of binomial coefficients with Pascal's rule.

solution.complexity: Time O(n^2) for the table and O(n) for the search, space O(n^2).
